evidence: Cic. Amic. 64: amīcus certus in rē incertā cernitur (Ennius)
terms.comment: The plain word, for a friend of any age; the vocative amīce is the “friend!” of the fables.
Lewis & Short calls this sense “very rare”: in comedy an amīca is usually a man’s mistress. Harmless for a small girl’s friends; sodālis or aequālis avoids the overtone.

terms.grammar: noun, third declension, masculine or feminine
evidence: Plaut. Merc. 2.4.7: tuos amīcus et sodālis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A favourite word of Plautus; Lewis & Short gives it common gender.

terms.gloss: a child of the same age; playmate
terms.grammar: noun, third declension, masculine or feminine
evidence: Plin. Ep. 9.33.4: redditque terrae et aequālibus
terms.comment: The friends a small child plays with are his age-mates.
Pliny’s word for the dolphin that played with the boys of Hippo; in Cicero, a partner at dice.

evidence: Ter. Ph. 5.8.60; 1.1.1; Ter. And. 5.6.6: amīcus summus, the best friend (Lewis & Short), s.v. superus
Traupman p. 98: amīca summa mea est

phrases.latin: vetus verbum hoc quidem est: commūnia esse amīcōrum inter sē omnia
phrases.english: it’s an old saying: friends share everything

phrases.latin: deinde aequālibus dēlectantur libenterque sē cum iīs congregant dantque sē ad lūdendum
phrases.english: then they enjoy children of their own age, gladly join them and give themselves up to play
